mcqs.question: A team splits its codebase into cleanly-bounded internal packages with enforced module boundaries, but still ships it as a single deployable process. What is this called, and what does it NOT give the team?
options: A modular monolith — it gives clean internal structure but not independent deployability per module
A microservices architecture — it gives every benefit of microservices with none of the network cost
A distributed monolith — it gives independent deployability but no clean boundaries
A service mesh — it gives traffic control between the internal packages
mcqs.explanation: A modular monolith keeps one deployment unit while enforcing internal boundaries, which improves maintainability but still means every module ships together — you don't get independent deploys, which is the thing microservices actually buys you. It isn't a microservices architecture, a distributed monolith, or a service mesh.

mcqs.question: A 4-person startup with one small codebase is deciding between a monolith and microservices for their MVP. Based on the velocity vs complexity trade-off, which is the stronger default?
options: Microservices, because they will need to scale to millions of users eventually
Monolith, because one small team shipping one codebase gets higher early velocity with far less operational overhead
Microservices, because failure isolation matters most at the MVP stage
Neither — they should use a serverless-only architecture regardless of team size
mcqs.explanation: At small team size, the monolith's simplicity dominates: no inter-service network design, one deploy pipeline, one thing to monitor. Microservices' benefits (independent team velocity, failure isolation) only pay off once multiple teams are actually blocking each other — a hypothetical future scale isn't a reason to pay the tax today, and serverless is an orthogonal choice, not a substitute for this decision.

mcqs.question: Per Conway's Law, what typically happens if a company splits its services in a way that cuts across three existing teams' ownership, instead of aligning with team boundaries?
options: The services deploy faster since there are more of them
The organization automatically reorganizes its teams to match the new services
The teams recreate the monolith's coordination cost across services, now with added network latency
Conway's Law predicts no organizational effect from service boundaries
mcqs.explanation: Conway's Law says systems mirror communication structure — so a boundary that cuts across existing teams forces those teams to keep coordinating a joint release, just like a monolith would, except now they also pay for network calls between the split pieces. Splitting services doesn't automatically speed up deploys or reorganize teams on its own.

mcqs.question: A 5-engineer startup adopts microservices because "Netflix and Amazon do it." What is the most likely real-world consequence?
options: Their system automatically becomes more scalable and reliable than before
Their deploy velocity roughly doubles immediately
Their database load drops because data is now split across services
The same small team now debugs outages across many network hops instead of one process, without enough people to staff per-service on-call
mcqs.explanation: Microservices add a fixed operational tax — service discovery, distributed tracing, per-service on-call — that a 5-person team can't fully staff, so an outage becomes harder to debug across many services rather than easier. Scalability and reliability aren't automatic, deploy velocity doesn't reliably double at this size, and database load isn't the driving concern here.
